meta.name: NSW Procurement Navigator knowledge base
meta.disclaimer: This tool summarises publicly available NSW procurement guidance and NSW Government procurement training material. It is general information, not legal or procurement advice. Always confirm against your own agency or council policy, the current Procurement Policy Framework, and the current legislation before you act.

primary_sources.label: Office of Local Government - Procurement in Local Government

meta.training_source: Procurement Foundations course, NSW Comperio (buy.nsw training). Eight modules were scraped and converted into the topic chunks in this knowledge base.

audiences.label: Local council
audiences.short: Council staff, procurement officers, business leads, joint organisations
audiences.blurb: Councils do not sit under the NSW Procurement Board framework. You are governed by the Local Government Act 1993 (ss 55, 55A), the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021 Part 7, and the Office of Local Government guidelines.

audiences.label: NSW Government agency buyer
audiences.short: Public servants procuring goods and services for a NSW Government agency
audiences.blurb: You work under the Public Works and Procurement Act 1912, the NSW Procurement Policy Framework, and NSW Procurement Board Directions. Your agency's accreditation level caps what you can procure.

audiences.label: Supplier or SME
audiences.short: Small and medium businesses, sole traders, start-ups, regional suppliers
audiences.blurb: You want to find, bid for and deliver NSW public sector work. NSW policy actively preferences SMEs, regional, Aboriginal and social enterprise suppliers below certain thresholds.

audiences.label: Corporate or large supplier
audiences.short: Prime contractors, tier-1 suppliers, multinationals, consortium leads
audiences.blurb: Above the larger thresholds you take on extra obligations: shorter payment terms to your small business subcontractors, SME participation criteria, modern slavery due diligence and local market testing.

audiences.label: Not-for-profit, social enterprise or Aboriginal business
audiences.short: Social enterprises, ADEs, disability employment organisations, Aboriginal-owned businesses
audiences.blurb: There are direct-engagement pathways that let buyers come to you without a full tender, but you generally need to be recognised by an approved body first.

audiences.blurb: You want to understand how public money is spent, what has to be disclosed, and how to raise a concern about a procurement.

thresholds.label: Up to $10,000 (ex GST)
thresholds.rule: A NSW Government agency may procure goods and services up to $10,000 (ex GST) from any supplier, even where the item is available on a whole-of-government arrangement. Purchases at this level should be made on a purchasing card (PCard) under the Faster Payment Terms Policy, subject to your agency's own PCard thresholds. You still need approval from a financial delegate, and you still need to record the value for money reasoning.

thresholds.label: Up to $50,000 direct from a small business
thresholds.rule: NSW Government agencies may purchase goods or services up to $50,000 directly from a small business, even where those goods or services are available on a whole-of-government arrangement. A small business for this purpose has fewer than 20 full-time equivalent employees.

thresholds.label: Up to $150,000 direct from a regional supplier
thresholds.rule: A NSW Government agency may buy directly from a regional supplier for procurements under $150,000.

thresholds.label: $150,000 (inc GST) - public contract disclosure
thresholds.rule: Under the Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009 you must publicly disclose contracts valued at $150,000 (inc GST) or more. Agencies disclose on NSW eTendering within 45 working days of the contract taking effect, and the entry stays listed for at least 20 days or until the contract is complete, whichever is longer. Councils maintain a public contracts register under section 27 of the GIPA Act on the same $150,000 (inc GST) trigger, published within 45 days and kept available for 20 working days or until contract obligations are satisfied, whichever is longer.

citations.label: IPC NSW - Register of government contracts

thresholds.label: Up to $250,000 - first consideration to Aboriginal business
thresholds.rule: Under the Aboriginal Procurement Policy, NSW Government agencies must give first consideration to Aboriginal businesses for procurements up to $250,000, and may buy directly from them, even where a mandated scheme or panel exists. An Aboriginal business for this purpose has at least 50 per cent Aboriginal ownership and is recognised through an appropriate organisation such as Supply Nation, the NSW Indigenous Chamber of Commerce, or the Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations.

thresholds.label: $250,000 (inc GST) - council tendering threshold
thresholds.rule: Section 55 of the Local Government Act 1993 requires a council to invite tenders before entering into a contract. Section 55(3)(n) exempts contracts involving estimated expenditure or receipt of less than $250,000. The threshold was raised from $100,000 to $250,000 by the Local Government Amendment Act 2019. Note this is a council rule and is entirely separate from the NSW Procurement Board thresholds that apply to state agencies.

thresholds.label: $680,000 - unaccredited agency ceiling and EPP trigger
thresholds.rule: Two separate rules sit near this figure. First, an unaccredited NSW Government agency can generally procure goods and services not available on whole-of-government arrangements up to about $680,000; above that it needs concurrence on its procurement strategy from an accredited agency in its portfolio or from NSW Procurement. Second, the enforceable procurement provisions in PBD-2019-05 generally apply where the estimated value exceeds $680,000 (ex GST) for goods and services, or $9.584 million (ex GST) for construction.

thresholds.label: $3 million - SME first preference and mandatory non-price criteria
thresholds.rule: Under the SME and Regional Procurement Policy, agencies must give first preference to SMEs for direct procurements up to $3 million, including when buying from a prequalification scheme or panel. For contracts over $3 million the policy sets mandatory minimum non-price evaluation criteria; agencies may apply those criteria below the threshold as well. An SME is an Australian or New Zealand based enterprise with fewer than 200 full-time equivalent employees.

thresholds.label: $7.5 million - local market testing and shorter payment terms
thresholds.rule: For projects worth more than $7.5 million, agencies must engage with local NSW suppliers before going to tender and must embed upfront local market testing in the procurement plan under PBD-2024-02. Separately, large businesses holding NSW Government goods and services contracts over $7.5 million must pay small businesses they directly subcontract within 20 business days of a correctly rendered invoice, under the Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy; model contract clauses should be used for these contracts.

citations.label: PBD-2024-02 Increasing opportunities for local suppliers
Small Business Shorter Payment Terms Policy

thresholds.label: 5 business days - small business invoice payment
thresholds.rule: Correctly rendered invoices between $10,000 and $1 million from registered small businesses (fewer than 20 FTE) must be paid within 5 business days under the Faster Payment Terms Policy. Invoices under $10,000 should be paid as soon as possible, ideally instantly by PCard.

citations.label: What is a correctly rendered invoice

thresholds.label: Agency accreditation ceilings
thresholds.rule: Level 1 accredited agencies may procure goods and services not available on whole-of-government arrangements up to $50 million for low risk, $35 million for medium risk and $20 million for high risk procurements; above those values they need concurrence from a level 2 agency in their portfolio or from NSW Procurement. Level 2 accredited agencies may procure any value within budget and play a concurrence role for their portfolio. Unaccredited agencies are generally capped at about $680,000.

thresholds.label: $150,000 (inc GST) - council modern slavery reporting
thresholds.rule: Councils have been required to take reasonable steps to ensure goods and services they procure are not the product of modern slavery since 1 July 2022. From 1 July 2024, a council must file an online report with the Office of the NSW Anti-slavery Commissioner within 45 days of a contract taking effect where that contract arose from a heightened modern slavery due diligence process and is valued at $150,000 (inc GST) or more.

citations.label: OLG circular 23-17 - councils' obligations under the Modern Slavery Act

thresholds.label: 21 days - minimum council tender period
thresholds.rule: Under the Local Government (General) Regulation 2021, a council's tender deadline must be at least 21 days after the date the advertisement is first published. In selective tendering under clause 168, the same 21-day minimum applies again to the invitation to tender issued to shortlisted applicants.

thresholds.label: 25 days - recommended agency tender period
thresholds.rule: For NSW Government agencies, allow a minimum of 25 calendar days when you publish a tender on NSW eTendering. Ten calendar days is the minimum recommended where the procurement was published in your agency's annual procurement plan within the last 12 months, where you are buying through approved arrangements such as a prequalification scheme, or for recurring procurement arrangements. There is no set minimum for genuinely urgent or emergency procurements. Covered procurements over $680,000 have their own minimum tender periods under the EPP Direction.

thresholds.label: 5 years - normal maximum contract term
thresholds.rule: As a general rule you should not make a contract run longer than 5 years, including any extension options. Whole-of-government contracts typically run for 3 years with 1 or 2 year extension options.

templates.name: Request for Information (RFI) and Response template
templates.description: Use when you need to understand the market before committing to a procurement approach. Does not commit you to buy.

templates.name: Expression of Interest (EOI) and Response template
templates.description: Use as stage one of a multi-stage approach to shortlist capable suppliers before inviting tenders. No pricing, no contract award.

templates.name: Opportunity Specific Terms and Conditions
templates.description: Part of the buy.nsw Opportunity suite. Sets the conditions of the market approach itself.

templates.name: Opportunity Information and Statement of Requirements
templates.description: Describes what you are buying and the requirements suppliers must respond to.

templates.name: Opportunity Response Document
templates.description: The response template you give suppliers so offers arrive in a consistent, comparable form.

templates.name: Addendum to Opportunity / RFx template
templates.description: Use to formally amend a live market approach. Give suppliers reasonable time to re-submit and notify everyone who downloaded the documents.

templates.name: Evaluation plan template
templates.description: Must be finalised before the tender closes and before you open any responses.

templates.name: Procurement conduct plan (conflicts of interest) template
templates.description: Sets the probity rules for your evaluation team and captures conflict of interest declarations before the market approach opens.

templates.name: Evaluation report template
templates.description: Documents the evaluation team's assessment and recommendation for contract award.

templates.name: Evaluation scoresheet
templates.description: Scoring sheet with guidance on how to rate how well a response meets your requirements.

templates.name: Shorter Payment Terms Policy - model contract clauses
templates.description: Use in goods and services contracts over $7.5 million so head contractors pay small business subcontractors within 20 business days.

templates.name: NSW Government contract templates
templates.description: Standard terms and conditions. Use an existing template where one exists; get legal advice before modifying one or negotiating new terms.

templates.name: Contract clauses and requirements guidance
templates.description: Guidance on insurances, indemnity, intellectual property, reporting and termination clauses.

templates.name: Guide to Environmentally Sustainable Procurement
templates.description: Practical templates and NSW agency case studies for building environmental sustainability into planning, sourcing and managing.

templates.name: ICAC - Supplier Due Diligence: a guide for NSW public sector agencies
templates.description: The reference document for what checks to run on a supplier, when, and by whom. Covers the five check categories and online verification techniques.

templates.name: ICAC - Managing conflicts of interest in the NSW public sector
templates.description: How to identify, declare and manage conflicts of interest, including the reasonable person test.

templates.name: Guidance on Reasonable Steps (modern slavery)
templates.description: NSW Anti-slavery Commissioner guidance on managing modern slavery risks in operations and supply chains. Operative from 1 January 2024.

templates.name: Tendering Guidelines for NSW Local Government
templates.description: Adopted under section 23A of the Local Government Act 1993, so councils must take them into consideration when exercising tendering functions. OLG has been developing replacement Procurement Guidelines - check the OLG site for the current version before relying on the 2009 document.

templates.name: NSW Procurement Board Complaint Management Guidelines
templates.description: How procurement complaints are handled, and the difference between covered procurement complaints under the EPP Direction and general procurement complaints.

templates.name: buy.nsw Supplier Hub
templates.description: Where suppliers register a profile and where buyers search for suppliers, including verified Aboriginal, disability employment, social enterprise and gender equitable identifiers.

templates.name: NSW eTendering (tenders.nsw.gov.au)
templates.description: Where agencies advertise and manage tenders, request quotes from scheme suppliers, and publish awarded contracts over $150,000 (inc GST).

templates.name: buy.nsw prequalification schemes
templates.description: Lists of assessed suppliers by category or capability. Some are mandatory for agencies, others recommended. Schemes generally do not include pricing, so value for money still has to be tested.

templates.name: NSW Government whole-of-government contracts
templates.description: The catalogue of whole-of-government contracts agencies must generally use where one is available.

templates.name: Local Government Procurement (LGP) approved contracts
templates.description: LGP is prescribed under section 55 of the Local Government Act 1993, so a council can buy from an LGP-established contract above $250,000 without running its own tender.

glossary.definition: An ongoing NSW Procurement Board assessment that authorises a government agency to procure goods and services up to a set value. Level 2 is the highest. Councils are not accredited under this scheme.
An invoice that meets the requirements set out in the contract or purchase order, so payment clocks such as the 5-business-day Faster Payment Terms rule start running.

A procurement caught by the enforceable procurement provisions in PBD-2019-05, generally above $680,000 (ex GST) for goods and services or $9.584 million (ex GST) for construction, giving suppliers enforceable rights.
Expression of interest. A first-stage market approach that shortlists capable suppliers. No pricing and no contract award at this stage.
NSW Procurement Board Direction PBD-2019-05, which implements Australia's international trade agreement obligations in NSW procurement.
Government Information (Public Access) Act 2009. Creates a public right to government information and requires public disclosure of contracts of $150,000 (inc GST) or more.
Also called piggybacking. A procurement arrangement set up by one agency that other agencies are permitted to use.
Purchasing card. A government credit card used for low value purchases, typically under $10,000, which removes the need to raise a purchase order.
A list of suppliers assessed as capable in defined categories, sometimes called a procurement list. Using one streamlines a competitive process but does not by itself prove value for money.
Acting ethically, with integrity, uprightness and honesty. In procurement it means value for money, impartiality, consistency and fairness, and accountability and transparency.
A commercial document issued by a buyer to a seller. It becomes a legally binding contract once the seller accepts it. Often used where no standalone contract is issued.
Umbrella term for market approach documents: RFI, EOI, RFQ, RFP and RFT.

Small or medium enterprise. Under the SME and Regional Procurement Policy, an Australian or New Zealand based business with fewer than 200 full-time equivalent employees. Small is 1 to 19 FTE, medium is 20 to 199 FTE.
For the Faster Payment Terms Policy and the $50,000 direct purchase rule, a business with fewer than 20 full-time equivalent employees.
A proposal put to government that was not requested through a market approach. In NSW these must be referred to the Department of Premier and Cabinet.
Total lifetime benefit minus total lifetime cost. Not the lowest price and not the highest quality, but fit for purpose at the lowest whole-of-life cost.
A contract appointing one or more suppliers to supply any NSW Government agency, usually for 3 years with extension options. Agencies must generally use one where available unless exempt.
